clinicalPearls: Intestinal capillariasis is caused by the nematode Capillaria philippinensis, acquired by eating raw or undercooked small freshwater or brackish-water fish, and is endemic to parts of Southeast Asia
It is a potentially fatal helminthiasis, distinguished from most intestinal worms by its ability to build up enormous worm numbers through internal autoinfection
The illness presents with chronic watery diarrhoea, borborygmi, abdominal pain and progressive weight loss
Severe infection causes a protein-losing enteropathy with malabsorption, leading to hypoproteinaemia, electrolyte depletion, muscle wasting and oedema, and death if untreated
Diagnosis rests on identifying the characteristic peanut-shaped eggs, larvae or adult worms in the stool, sometimes requiring repeated examination
Because autoinfection sustains and amplifies the burden, prolonged anthelmintic courses are needed rather than a single dose
Albendazole or mebendazole given as an extended course is the mainstay, together with correction of fluid, electrolyte and protein deficits
reference.pathophysiology: Capillaria philippinensis normally cycles between fish-eating birds and freshwater fish, with humans infected by consuming raw fish containing infective larvae. The larvae mature into adults that burrow into the mucosa of the small intestine. Crucially, the females can produce larvae that develop in situ and reinvade the same host's intestine, a process of internal autoinfection that allows the worm population to multiply to very large numbers over time. This heavy mucosal infestation damages the small-bowel epithelium, causing villous atrophy and a severe protein-losing enteropathy with malabsorption of nutrients, protein and electrolytes; the resulting hypoproteinaemia, wasting, oedema and electrolyte disturbance account for the potentially fatal course of untreated disease.
additionalDifferentials: Giardiasis and other malabsorptive protozoal infections
Chronic infective diarrhoea from other pathogens
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for characteristic eggs, larvae and adult worms
Repeated stool examination given intermittent and sometimes scanty shedding
Serum albumin and total protein to assess protein loss
Full blood count and assessment of nutritional status
Small-bowel biopsy when stool examination is repeatedly negative
redFlags: Relapse after apparently successful treatment due to ongoing autoinfection
reference.prognosis: Untreated heavy infection is frequently fatal, but with an adequate prolonged anthelmintic course and correction of protein, fluid and electrolyte deficits the outlook is good, though relapse can occur if treatment is too short.
pitfalls: Giving a single short anthelmintic course, which fails to control autoinfection and permits relapse
Missing the diagnosis when stool shedding is scanty and only one sample is examined
Attributing chronic diarrhoea and wasting to other malabsorptive disease without stool parasitology in endemic areas
Underestimating the severity of fluid, electrolyte and protein losses
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Prolonged anthelmintic therapy with albendazole (or mebendazole) extended well beyond symptom resolution to overcome internal autoinfection
Correction of protein, fluid and electrolyte deficits arising from the protein-losing enteropathy
Nutritional support to reverse wasting and the malabsorption of nutrients
Monitoring of serum albumin, total protein and electrolytes alongside clinical response during and after treatment
Repeat stool examination to confirm clearance and detect relapse, extending therapy if worms persist
Advice on avoiding raw or undercooked freshwater and brackish-water fish to prevent reinfection
Inpatient escalation for severe hypoproteinaemia, oedema or electrolyte disturbance
